key_concept: The brain and spinal cord are covered by three meninges (dura mater, arachnoid and pia mater), whereas the pericardium is the double-layered sac around the heart.
steps: The central neural system (CNS) consists of the brain and spinal cord, which are protected by three cranial or spinal meninges.
Dura mater is the outer, tough meningeal layer, so it belongs to the CNS coverings.
Arachnoid is the thin middle meningeal layer, so it also belongs to the CNS coverings.
Pia mater is the delicate inner meningeal layer, in contact with the brain tissue, so it too belongs to the CNS coverings.
Pericardium is the double-walled membranous sac enclosing the heart. It is part of the circulatory system, not the neural system.
Therefore pericardium is not a part of the human central neural system.
why_not_others: Arachnoid, dura mater and pia mater are the three meninges that cover the brain and spinal cord, so all three are CNS structures. Only the pericardium belongs to another organ system (the heart).
common_trap: Students sometimes confuse membrane names across systems (meninges, pleura, pericardium) and doubt whether 'arachnoid' is a valid meningeal layer.
time_saving_tip: Remember the meninges from outer to inner as 'DAP' (Dura, Arachnoid, Pia). Any membrane outside this trio is the odd one out.
